title: Tradeweb Government Bond Update – October 2026
summary: Global government bond markets rallied in October, reversing three consecutive months of sell-offs. Yields fell across most major markets, as concerns over AI-related spending and volatility in technology shares supported demand for government debt.
body_markdown:
Global government bond markets rallied in October, reversing three consecutive months of sell-offs. Yields fell across most major markets, as concerns over AI-related spending and volatility in technology shares supported demand for government debt.


The biggest mover was Japan’s 10-year government bond yield; it fell 29 basis points to end the month at 2.77%, after reaching 3.13% on October 1, a level last seen in 1996. The Bank of Japan left its policy rate unchanged at 1.25% on October 30 in an 8–1 vote, while expectations of another increase in December remained in focus.


Taichi Shibuya, Head of Japan at Tradeweb, said: “Japanese government bond yields retreated in October after touching their highest level in three decades at the start of the month. The move highlights how sensitive Japanese yields remain to global interest rate dynamics, domestic investor demand, and changing policy expectations.”


Elsewhere in Asia Pacific, Australia’s 10-year benchmark bond yield declined 20 basis points to 5.15%. Quarterly trimmed mean inflation accelerated to 3.7% year-on-year in the September quarter, exceeding the Reserve Bank of Australia’s expectations.


In the U.S., the 10-year Treasury yield fell 25 basis points to close October at 4.91%. The Federal Reserve maintained its target range at 3.75%–4.00% on October 28, with two members dissenting in favour of a 25-basis point hike. Canada’s 10-year government bond yield declined 13 basis points to 3.78%. The Bank of Canada raised its policy rate by 25 basis points to 2.50% on October 28.


Across the Atlantic, the European Central Bank left its deposit rate unchanged at 2.50% on October 29. President Christine Lagarde said policymakers had discussed an increase, but unanimously agreed to hold rates pending further data. Preliminary Eurostat figures showed that the euro area economy expanded by 0.4% in the third quarter compared with the previous three months.


France bucked the broader rally, with its 10-year government bond yield rising 13 basis points to 4.97%. The yield reached 5.14% on October 22, its highest level since July 2002. The country’s private sector returned to contraction, with the flash composite PMI falling to 48.4 in October. Moody’s left France’s Aa3 sovereign rating and negative outlook unchanged following its October 23 review.


Preliminary data showed that Germany’s economy grew by 0.2% in the third quarter. The 10-year Bund yield ended October 26 basis points lower at 3.32%, while its Italian equivalent finished at 4.51%. According to initial estimates from Istat, Italy’s economy was unchanged in the third quarter compared with the previous three months. Meanwhile, annual harmonised inflation accelerated to an estimated 5.6% in October.


Greece’s 10-year benchmark yield declined 16.6 basis points to 4.30%; S&P maintained the country’s BBB rating with a stable outlook at its October 23 review. Sweden’s 10-year government bond yield fell 13 basis points to 3.10%, while the Riksbank’s policy rate remained at 1.75%.


In the UK, Gilt markets showed a muted reaction to Chancellor John Healey’s Budget on October 28. The 10-year Gilt yield finished the month at 5.29%, after reaching 5.52% on October 8, its highest level since 2007. Annual CPI inflation increased to 3.5% in September from 3.1% in August, keeping attention on the Bank of England’s November 5 decision.
